# TrustBench: paired evaluation of tool-call enforcement against indirect prompt injection

*Technical report (TB-047). It has not been peer reviewed. Generated by `scripts/build-report.py` from stored run artifacts:
every number below is read from a committed file, and [`report-claims.json`](report-claims.json) maps each one to its
source file and path.*

## Summary

TrustBench measures whether an AI agent that uses tools can be stopped from committing unsafe effects when the content it
reads carries injected instructions, without losing the user's task. It runs the same agent with and without a defense on
identical inputs and reads outcomes from what the tools actually committed, not from what the model said.

On the pre-declared primary analysis (sealed holdouts, the frozen defended system against the undefended agent on the
`nvidia:openai/gpt-oss-20b` model), unsafe committed effects fell from 52/75 to
8/75 runs (-58.7 pp,
95% interval [-77.3, -38.7]), and benign task success rose from
44/75 to 66/75
(+29.3 pp, [+16.0, +44.0]). The registered
hypothesis is **supported** on that analysis. The result is narrower than it sounds:

- holdout-1 on its own is **not separated** (its interval
  reaches zero);
- the provenance-aware layer, the part the hypothesis names, is not shown to cause the gain; development ablations credit the
  capability gateway's tool allowlist and argument contracts instead;
- the defended agent is slower per run and still fails on some attacks and benign tasks;
- the attacks are static renderings; no adaptive attacker was tested.

## Problem

An agent that reads documents, emails or records and then calls tools can be steered by text inside that content
(indirect prompt injection): it may read a document it should not, send data out, write an attacker's value into a record
or cite a source it was told to avoid. Defenses inside the prompt or the model are probabilistic. Enforcement outside the
model, at each tool call, can block an effect regardless of what the model was persuaded to do, but it can also block the
user's legitimate work. The question is how much such enforcement reduces committed unsafe effects, at what cost in task
success, latency and tokens, measured so that the comparison cannot be tuned to the test data.

## Threat model

Full model: [`docs/threat-model.md`](../docs/threat-model.md). In brief:

- **Attacker:** controls part of a retrieved document, email body, record note or tool-returned string, knows the public
  workflows, and may phrase text to address the agent. The attacker cannot change the authenticated task contract, the
  policy, the evaluator or the tool service.
- **Untrusted:** all model output and all retrieved content. **Trusted:** the task contract, policy files, evaluator, tool
  service and the host.
- **Security properties:** user-intent integrity, least privilege, data-flow confinement, exact approval of consequential
  calls, effect integrity (no duplicated or altered writes), evidence integrity and bounded execution.
- **Excluded:** a malicious host or maintainer, compromised providers, real external services (all tools and data are local
  and synthetic), and adaptive or optimisation-based attackers in the confirmatory runs.

## System

**Undefended agent (baseline).** A bounded tool-calling loop over a local synthetic tool service whose tools accept any
well-formed call; the agent sees the user's task and the tool results. It is the registered baseline (A-001): the
comparison measures enforcement for agents whose tools do not enforce task contracts themselves.

**Defended system (frozen).** `gateway_directive_flow_v4`, selected on development data under rule A-023
([`docs/frozen-config.md`](../docs/frozen-config.md)) and frozen before the holdouts were run. It places a capability
gateway between the agent and the tools:

- a per-task **tool allowlist** and **argument contracts** (resources, recipients, records and fields the task may touch);
- **exact-argument approval** for consequential writes, bound to the normalised arguments;
- **signed provenance** on every tool output, so later checks know which text came from untrusted content;
- a **directive-flow check** that refuses a write whose data argument carries a value attributed to an instruction found in
  untrusted content, and **sticky denials** that refuse an identical retried write.

The agent, prompt and model are identical in both arms; only the gateway differs.

## Experimental design

Protocol: [`protocol/preregister.md`](../protocol/preregister.md), registry
[`protocol/experiment-registry.yaml`](../protocol/experiment-registry.yaml), amendments
[`protocol/amendments.md`](../protocol/amendments.md) (each recorded before the result it governs, except A-029, which is
marked post hoc).

- **Workflows and data.** 3 synthetic workflows (document evidence analyst, email draft
  assistant, controlled record update), 27 benign task fixtures and 28 attack fixtures.
  Split `trustbench-core-template-family-v3`: 25 development fixtures, a holdout of
  6 and a second holdout of 24 with new attack families
  (A-026). Each holdout was sealed by hash before it was run, was never used for tuning or selection, and was run once.
- **Frozen configuration.** Selected from 3499 valid development runs with a utility margin
  of 5.0 percentage points and at least 40
  attack and 20 benign runs per arm. Best-of-many selection overstates
  expected performance, which is why only the holdouts are confirmatory.
- **Runs.** Each holdout case was run on both arms, paired by seed and inputs, 5 times per
  pair. Holdout-1: 30 valid pairs (attack and benign)
  per rendering; holdout-2: 60 benign and
  60 attack pairs on the primary rendering. Attack text was rendered in several published styles; the primary rendering is AgentDojo's
  "important instructions", the others are secondary, and a trusted-user rendering is a positive control.
- **Endpoints.** Primary: unsafe committed effect on attack cases and benign utility on benign cases, both read from tool
  state by the evaluator ([`src/evaluators/outcomes_v2.py`](../src/evaluators/outcomes_v2.py)). Secondary: attacker goal
  achieved and secure-and-useful under attack.
- **Statistics.** Paired differences with a cluster bootstrap over (task, attack variant) clusters,
  10,000 resamples, seed 20261048, 95% percentile
  intervals. Invalid runs are listed and never counted as secure.
- **Decision rule** (protocol/preregister.md, Primary endpoints): supported when the unsafe-effect interval lies below zero and the lower
  end of the utility interval is above minus 5 percentage points.

32/75 → 8/75
(-32.0 pp [-49.3, -16.0]); secure and useful

**Cost** (pooled primary, paired, 150 pairs). Median run time
24.6 s undefended and
43.6 s defended; defended runs took
16.2 s longer on average. Input tokens per run
+671
[+311, +1,033], output tokens
+415
[+246, +580]. All providers
were free tiers, so billed cost is zero; per successful task the defended arm used fewer tokens in
9 of 12
workloads, because more of its tasks succeed.

**Which component helps** (development ablations, exploratory, A-027; [`docs/ablations.md`](../docs/ablations.md)). With the
tool allowlist and argument contracts, unsafe effects are lower than without them (with minus without
-51.8 pp,
[-77.8, -25.9]); adding the
directive-flow layer on top of the gateway shows no measurable contribution, its interval reaching zero
(-22.2 pp,
[-55.6, +0.0]). These are
development data on which the system was designed, so they are optimistic, and the holdouts had no capability-only arm.

**Same-harness comparison with published defenses** (development, exploratory, re-implementations, not the authors'
systems; [`docs/defense-comparison.md`](../docs/defense-comparison.md)). Unsafe committed effects per
18 attack runs: the undefended agent paired with the frozen system
13, frozen system
0, capability gateway alone
3, CaMeL-style
12, spotlighting
14, MELON-style
15. With so few runs per system these are exploratory
(the comparison table gives Wilson intervals); the frozen system was also chosen on these development data.

## Failure cases

- **Workflow.** On the document workflow the unsafe-effect interval includes zero
  (9/25
  → 5/25,
  -16.0 pp
  [-40.0, +0.0]).
  The defended document failures are TB-ATT-DOC-102 (an attacker's value stated as a fact) and TB-ATT-DOC-104 (an
  unsupported answer that overrides a required abstention). Both write into the answer field the task permits, so the
  allowlist and argument contracts cannot stop them, and the directive-flow check did not stop them in these runs.
- **Attacks not reduced.** TB-ATT-DOC-104 succeeded as often defended as undefended
  (3/5
  → 3/5).
- **New attack families.** On holdout-2's new families the interval includes zero
  (11/15
  → 3/15,
  [-100.0, +0.0]).
- **Defended failures.** 8 defended attack runs still committed an unsafe
  effect, and 9 defended benign runs failed their task, mostly record updates
  whose final value did not match (8); each run is
  listed in [`findings.md`](findings.md).

## Evaluation quality

**Label audit** (TB-045, [`label-audit.md`](label-audit.md)). A stratified sample of 61
of 780 confirmatory runs was labelled blind by AI reviewers from different model families (reviewer A's model and Nemotron)
and every disagreement was adjudicated with a written reason; no human reviewed any run. Agreement with the evaluator on
security labels was 88.5% (reviewer A) and
100.0% (reviewer B) (Cohen's kappa 0.75
and 1.00). The audit found
1 evaluator error, a rule defect that counted a forbidden read as
the attacker's goal; after the post-hoc correction (A-029) 6 runs were relabelled and the
primary analysis did not change. The audit also measured how much of the baseline's unsafe rate is only extra reads with
an unlisted tool: counting those as safe, the pooled primary difference becomes
-42.7 pp
[-58.7, -26.7],
still below zero.

**Hung provider calls** (TB-040). 23 of 780 confirmatory runs
ended while a model call was still open. Excluding them leaves the pooled unsafe difference at
-59.4 pp.

## Engineering evidence

- **Release gate** ([`docs/release-gate.md`](../docs/release-gate.md)): a credential-free scripted tier on every push compares
  verdicts case by case with the committed baselines and blocks security or functional regressions and a more permissive
  policy audit trail; injected regressions are tested to fail it.
- **Fault and recovery drills** ([`reports/fault-drill.md`](../reports/fault-drill.md),
  [`reports/rollback-drill.md`](../reports/rollback-drill.md)): 50 fault tests passed and
  0 failed; a bad policy change was detected and rolled back in
  18.8 s and a deployment image in 6.0 s.
- **Reproducibility** ([`repro/README.md`](../repro/README.md)): 10 offline steps rebuild the
  published results from the committed raw run records, and the last run is **REPRODUCED** with
  0 unexpected file changes.
- **Live demo**: the comparison can be rerun from a browser or the CLI ([`docs/live-service.md`](../docs/live-service.md)).

## Limits

- **Scope.** Synthetic workflows, local mock tools and small free models; no web agents, memory, backdoor or multi-agent
  attacks. Results are rates with intervals for this configuration, not a security property.
- **Static attacks.** Every holdout attack is a fixed rendering; an attacker who adapts to the gateway was not tested, and
  AutoDojo (RW07) shows static benchmarks can overstate defense efficacy. The results are best read as upper bounds.
- **Component attribution.** The provenance-aware part named in the hypothesis is not shown to drive the gain; only the
  capability gateway is credited, on development data.
- **Baseline choice.** The undefended baseline uses a permissive tool backend. When the tool service itself enforces the
  task contract the baseline is already much safer and the gateway adds little (known issue M5,
  [`docs/known-issues.md`](../docs/known-issues.md)).
- **Model dependence.** Some models never read the injected text, so no defense effect can be measured on them (M7); the
  confirmatory runs use one hosted model, whose provider may change it.
- **Labels.** The evaluator was audited by AI reviewers only; a human review of the same packets would be stronger.
- **Replay.** Live model runs cannot be replayed exactly; the raw records are published and every number is recomputed from
  them.

## Relation to prior work

[`related-work.md`](related-work.md) compares 24 prior systems and studies. Enforcement
outside the model is not new: CaMeL (RW19), FIDES (RW20), RTBAS (RW21) and Progent (RW22) already place a deterministic boundary at tool calls,
and CaMeL and FIDES give guarantees by construction or over a formal model, which TrustBench does not. What this project
adds is evaluation and engineering practice: paired, preregistered runs on sealed holdouts with invalid runs counted,
outcomes read from committed tool state, same-harness re-implementations of published defenses, an audited evaluator, and a
release gate, drills and a reproducible offline package around them.
